young.html: In the Italian city of Verona live two families, the Montagues and the Capulets, who have hated each other for so long that no one remembers why. Their servants even fight in the street.

Romeo, a Montague, sneaks into a Capulet party and meets Juliet, a Capulet. They fall in love at once, before they even learn each other's names. Then, at night, Juliet stands at her window and wonders aloud why a name should matter so much.

young.text:
What's in a name? That which we call a rose
By any other name would smell as sweet.
young.author: William Shakespeare
young.work: Romeo and Juliet, Act II, scene 2 (Juliet)
young.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

young.html: They marry in secret, hoping to end the feud. But a street fight, a hasty choice, and a letter that never arrives lead to a sad ending: both young people die. Only then do their families, heartbroken, make peace.

For parents: the play has sword fights and ends with the deaths of the two young lovers by their own hands. Young readers can follow the story through Act II (the meeting, the balcony and the secret wedding) and a good retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

Slow down. Friar Laurence warns Romeo, "Wisely, and slow. They stumble that run fast." List every choice in the story that was made in a hurry. Then rewrite one of them: what if someone had waited a day?
young.title: Try this: change one choice

full.html: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet around 1595, early in his career. He took the plot from Arthur Brooke's long English poem The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet (1562), which came from Italian tales. He sped the story up from months to about four days, and gave the minor characters, Mercutio and the Nurse, unforgettable life.

full.text:
Two households, both alike in dignity,
In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.note: The first six of fourteen lines. "Civil" blood is citizens' blood. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: The prologue is a sonnet, fourteen lines rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, and it tells us the ending before the play begins. We watch knowing what the characters do not: this is dramatic irony, and it makes every hopeful moment ache.

full.html: When Romeo and Juliet first speak, their fourteen lines together make another sonnet, shared between them. Later, at her window, he compares her to the sun.

full.text:
But soft! What light through yonder window breaks?
It is the East, and Juliet is the sun!
full.author: William Shakespeare

full.html: The play turns in Act III. Mercutio, Romeo's friend, is killed by Tybalt; Romeo, in a rage, kills Tybalt and is banished. From then on, chance and haste work together: a forced engagement to Paris, the Friar's risky potion, a plague that stops his letter, and Romeo arriving at the tomb minutes too soon. Readers still argue whether the lovers are destroyed by fate ("star-cross'd"), by their own speed, or by the hatred of their elders.

Calling the play a simple love story. It is also about a city poisoned by an old feud, and about how young people pay for their elders' hatred. Juliet is not yet fourteen, and the adults around her mostly fail her.

deep.text: A tragedy that starts as a comedy

deep.html: The first two acts have the stuff of comedy: a party, a balcony, a witty friend, a comic Nurse, a secret wedding. Then Mercutio dies, and the play turns. Critics see Shakespeare testing what happens when comedy's young lovers meet a world that will not bend.

items: Is it fate, chance, or choice that destroys the lovers?
Is their love wise, or only young? Does it matter?
Why does it take a disaster to end the feud? Who is most to blame?

deep.html: Ovid's tale of Pyramus and Thisbe, two lovers separated by their parents, is an ancestor of this play, and Shakespeare mocked it lovingly in A Midsummer Night's Dream, written at about the same time.

questions: Juliet asks "What's in a name?" Can a name, or a family, make someone your enemy?
Who is most to blame for what happens: Romeo, Juliet, their parents, the Friar, or bad luck?
Friar Laurence says "They stumble that run fast." When has hurrying caused you trouble?
Why do you think the play tells us the ending in its very first speech?
care: Romeo and Juliet contains sword fights and ends with the deaths of the two young lovers by their own hands. This lesson states this plainly without detail. Young readers can focus on Acts I and II.
